description: A convincing message can create urgency, imitate a familiar service or appear to come from someone an employee trusts. Awareness advice is important, but organisations also need a way to practise recognition and understand where further guidance may help.

items.title: Prepare the organisation and audience
items.headline: Start with the right scope.
items.description: Set up your organisation and complete the required programme authorisation. Add employee records and organise them by department or other available employee attributes. Review consent and eligibility so that campaign targeting reflects the approved scope.
checklist: Confirm the business owner and purpose of the exercise.
Record the required Rules of Engagement or authorisation.
Add the employee records that belong in scope.
Review eligibility and consent requirements.

items.title: Select or create a template
items.headline: Match the message to the learning objective.
items.description: Choose a saved phishing template or create a new one. Add the subject, HTML body and plain-text version. Choose the lure type, category and difficulty, then use the preview to review the message before it is selected for a campaign.
checklist: Choose one clear learning objective.
Select a suitable message scenario.
Review the sender, subject and message content.
Confirm the tracking elements required by the campaign setup.
Preview and approve the template.

items.title: Configure and review the campaign
items.headline: Choose who receives it and when.
items.description: Create a campaign using the saved template. Name it, select the audience and choose the available targeting approach: all eligible employees, a segment or a sample percentage. Configure the delivery window and choose to send immediately or schedule the campaign. Review the campaign details before dispatch.
checklist: Confirm the saved template.
Set a clear campaign name.
Review the audience and eligibility.
Confirm the schedule and any stagger settings.
Check that email delivery is configured.
Review and dispatch only after final approval.
items.outcome: A campaign configured for the approved audience and schedule.

items.title: Review interactions
items.headline: Look at the event pattern, not just one number.
items.description: After delivery, review the campaign's available tracking events. Depending on the campaign setup, these may include sends, opens, link clicks, landing-page views and reported messages. Consider the limitations of email privacy tools and automated link scanners when interpreting results.
checklist: Confirm campaign delivery status.
Review the available event types and timestamps.
Investigate anomalies before drawing conclusions.
Compare patterns by department or campaign where appropriate.
Keep individual employee data limited to people who need it.
items.outcome: A contextual view of the campaign's interactions.

items.title: Report, coach and improve
items.headline: Turn the results into a useful next step.
items.description: Generate a campaign report where the campaign status makes reporting available. Review engagement metrics and relevant risk indicators, then decide whether the next step is a targeted training module, a team briefing, updated guidance or another simulation. Use training records to follow up on completion.
checklist: Generate the available campaign report.
Review risk insights and department-level trends.
Identify a small number of learning priorities.
Assign or organise relevant follow-up training.
Record completions where supported.
Use the learning to plan the next campaign.
items.outcome: A repeatable improvement cycle rather than a one-off test.

seo.title: Phause FAQs | Phishing Simulation & Awareness
seo.description: Get answers about Phause accounts, employee eligibility, phishing templates, campaigns, tracking, reporting, risk insights, training and responsible use.

items.question: What is Phause?
items.answer: Phause is a phishing simulation and security-awareness management platform. It helps organisations manage employee records, prepare phishing email templates, configure campaigns, review simulation interactions, generate reports and organise follow-up training.

items.question: Who is Phause designed for?
items.answer: Phause is designed for security leaders, IT administrators, security-awareness managers and organisations that want a more structured way to plan and review phishing-awareness exercises.

items.question: Is Phause a managed security operations service or endpoint protection tool?
items.answer: No. The product described here focuses on phishing simulations and security-awareness programme management. It should not be confused with endpoint detection, a managed SOC, a cloud firewall or a penetration-testing service.

items.question: How do I get started?
items.answer: Create an account, verify your email address, complete your organisation setup and prepare your authorised audience. Before launching a campaign, review the required Rules of Engagement or authorisation record and confirm employee eligibility.

items.question: Can I organise employees by department?
items.answer: Yes. Employee records can include department and seniority information, which helps your team organise the audience and use the available campaign targeting options.

items.question: Why does employee consent or eligibility matter?
items.answer: Campaigns should only target people who are within the approved scope and meet your organisation's consent and eligibility requirements. Review the employee record and campaign audience before dispatch.

items.question: Do I need to record authorisation before creating a campaign?
items.answer: The product includes an organisation authorisation or Rules of Engagement workflow. Campaign creation may be blocked until the required authorisation has been recorded. Follow your organisation's approval process before running a simulation.

items.question: Can I create my own phishing email templates?
items.answer: Yes. The template workflow supports a name, subject, HTML body and plain-text body, along with lure type, category and difficulty. You can preview the message before using it in a campaign.

items.question: What kinds of simulation scenarios can I organise?
items.answer: Template classifications include urgency, authority, curiosity and reward lure types, as well as categories such as credential-harvest simulation, attachment, link-click, awareness and data-entry scenarios. Choose a scenario that matches the learning objective and your approved scope.

items.question: Do I need to select a saved template before creating a campaign?
items.answer: Yes. The current campaign workflow starts by selecting a saved template. Create or save the template first, then use it to configure a campaign.

items.question: Can I choose who receives a campaign?
items.answer: Campaign targeting supports all eligible employees, a department segment or a sample percentage, subject to the options available to your organisation and plan. Always review the final audience before dispatch.

items.question: Can campaigns be scheduled?
items.answer: The campaign workflow supports immediate delivery and scheduled delivery. Review the date, time and audience carefully before confirming the campaign.

items.question: Can I cancel a campaign after dispatch?
items.answer: Campaign changes depend on the current campaign status. Draft or scheduled campaigns may have more editing options than campaigns that are already sending or sent. Use the controls shown in the campaign detail view.

items.question: What events can Phause track?
items.answer: Depending on the campaign and tracking configuration, events may include sent, email open, link click, landing-page view, reported message and training completion. The exact events available depend on the workflow used.

items.question: Are email opens and clicks always accurate?
items.answer: No tracking signal should be treated as perfect proof of human behaviour. Email privacy features and image proxies may cause opens to be recorded automatically or prevent them from appearing. Automated security scanners may also follow links. Interpret events in context and look for broader patterns.

items.question: Can I generate and download campaign reports?
items.answer: The reporting area supports campaign reports for eligible campaign statuses and includes export workflows for supported formats. The report detail view shows the campaign information and metrics available for that report.

items.question: What is an employee risk score?
items.answer: A risk score is a programme indicator intended to help prioritise follow-up awareness activity. It should not be used as a stand-alone judgement of an employee's character, competence or overall performance. Review the contributing context and use results constructively.

items.question: Does Phause provide training?
items.answer: Phause includes training administration features for managing module records, reviewing enrolments and recording completion history. The exact learning experience depends on the configured module content and your organisation's workflow.

items.question: How do I know what my plan includes?
items.answer: Review the plan and limits shown in your account or on the current pricing page. Employee limits, campaign limits and available capabilities can depend on the plan assigned to your organisation.

items.question: How do subscriptions and payments work?
items.answer: The billing workflow displays the subscription and payment options configured for your account. Review the billing period, currency, amount and subscription terms at checkout before confirming a payment. For account-specific questions, contact the Phause team.

items.question: Does Phause store real employee passwords?
items.answer: Phause's simulation landing flow is designed to record the interaction rather than retain actual submitted credential values. Do not configure exercises to collect real passwords, and verify the current landing-page settings before each campaign. The published Privacy Policy should explain precisely what event and employee data the live system processes.

items.question: How should we communicate simulations to employees?
items.answer: Follow your organisation's policies and approvals. Use a clear learning purpose, avoid humiliating or blaming individuals, and share practical guidance after the exercise. Keep employee-level results confidential and limit access to those who need it.

items.question: Can I use Phause to simulate messages outside my organisation?
items.answer: Only use Phause for exercises you are authorised to conduct. Do not target external people, organisations or systems without explicit permission and an agreed scope.

items.question: Where can I get help?
items.answer: Use the Contact page to send the Phause team an enquiry. For product workflows, start with the Documentation page. Do not include passwords, one-time verification codes or confidential employee information in a support message.

posts.contentHtml:
Awareness improves when people can practise

Employees receive messages throughout the day. Some are routine, some are urgent and some ask for an action that could expose information or create risk. A convincing phishing message can resemble an ordinary workplace request, which is why awareness needs to be more than an annual reminder.

A phishing simulation gives an organisation a controlled way to practise recognition. Instead of discussing suspicious messages only in theory, a team can observe how a simulated message is encountered and use the exercise as a starting point for learning.

What a simulation can help reveal

A well-planned exercise can help a programme owner explore questions such as:

  • Do employees pause when a message creates urgency?
  • Are there message patterns that consistently attract interactions?
  • Do employees know how to report a suspicious message?
  • Which teams may benefit from additional guidance?
  • Are follow-up learning activities reaching the intended audience?

These questions are more useful than treating one click as a verdict. A campaign is a snapshot of activity under specific conditions, not a complete picture of an employee's judgement or competence.

Build the exercise around a learning objective

Before choosing a template, decide what the organisation wants to practise. It may be recognising an unexpected attachment, checking a link destination, verifying a payment-related request or reporting a message that appears to come from a trusted source.

The learning objective should guide the template, audience, timing and follow-up. Avoid choosing a scenario only because it is likely to generate a high click rate. The aim is to improve awareness, not to trick employees for its own sake.

Use clear authorisation and scope

A responsible simulation begins before the message is sent. Confirm who approved the exercise, which employees are in scope, what internal teams need to know and how results will be handled. Review any consent and employee-communication requirements that apply to your organisation.

Coordinate with the people responsible for email security and help-desk operations so that reports or unusual behaviour can be handled sensibly. Avoid collecting real passwords or unnecessary personal information.

Interpret campaign signals with care

Opens and clicks can be useful signals, but they are not perfect measures of human behaviour. Email clients may block images, privacy tools may pre-load content, and automated security scanners may visit links. Review the event pattern, delivery context and other available information before drawing conclusions.

Use reports to identify themes and decide where a team conversation, short learning module or clearer reporting instructions could help.

Close the loop with learning

A simulation should lead to a useful next step. Share practical advice, make reporting routes clear and use the results to decide what the next awareness activity should cover. Follow-up should be constructive and respectful, not a public ranking of employees.

Repeat the programme at an appropriate cadence and compare trends over time. Look for sustained improvement and better reporting habits rather than focusing on one campaign's headline number.

How Phause can support the workflow

Phause brings employee management, phishing email templates, campaign setup, interaction tracking, campaign reporting, risk insights and training administration into one workspace. Teams can use the workflow to organise an authorised simulation and connect the outcome with follow-up learning.

Take the next step: Explore the Phause platform at /services or learn the workflow at /how-it-works.

posts.seoTitle: How to Interpret Phishing Simulation Opens and Clicks | Phause
posts.metaDescription: Learn why email opens and link clicks need context and how to use phishing simulation events responsibly when reviewing campaign performance.
posts.excerpt: Learn why email opens and link clicks need context and how to use phishing simulation events responsibly when reviewing campaign performance.

posts.featuredImageAlt: Campaign analytics dashboard with email interaction events and a report summary.
posts.contentHtml:
Metrics are signals, not the full story

A campaign report can make it easier to understand what happened during a phishing simulation. Sends, opens, link clicks, landing-page views and reported messages each describe a different part of the interaction.

It is tempting to treat a single number as the result. A more useful approach is to ask what the signal can tell you, what it cannot tell you and what additional context you need.

Email opens have limitations

Open tracking commonly relies on an image or tracking element being requested by an email client. Some clients block images. Others use privacy features or proxy services that load remote content automatically. As a result, an open event may not represent a person deliberately reading the message, and the absence of an open event does not necessarily mean the message was never seen.

Use open rates as one directional measure. Avoid using them as a precise measure of employee attention.

Link clicks can be automated

Organisations often use email-security services that inspect message links before delivery or when a message is received. Those systems may visit URLs automatically. A click event can therefore be generated by an automated scanner rather than a human recipient.

When reviewing clicks, consider timing, repeated requests, known scanning patterns and any additional event information available to your team. Do not assume every click proves a person interacted with the message.

Look at multiple indicators

Review the campaign as a whole. Consider delivery, different event types, employee reports, landing-page views and follow-up training records where available. Compare patterns across campaigns only when the audience, template, timing and tracking configuration are sufficiently similar.

Use the report to ask better questions

Rather than asking only whether the click rate went up or down, ask:

  • Which message themes generated the most interaction?
  • Did employees report the message through the expected route?
  • Did the campaign reach the intended audience?
  • Were there technical events that could affect the metrics?
  • Which topics should be included in the next learning activity?

Keep the human context

Simulation metrics should support learning, not replace judgement. One employee interaction should not define a person's overall security awareness. Use individual information only where there is a clear organisational need, and communicate findings constructively.

Phause provides campaign event views, reporting and risk insights to help teams review the available signals. Use those tools as part of a wider process that includes context, internal policy and practical follow-up.

posts.title: Turn Phishing Campaign Results into Better Learning
posts.seoTitle: Turn Phishing Campaign Results into Better Learning | Phause
posts.metaDescription: Learn how to use phishing simulation reports and employee engagement patterns to organise targeted, respectful security-awareness training.
posts.excerpt: Learn how to use phishing simulation reports and employee engagement patterns to organise targeted, respectful security-awareness training.
posts._excerptNote: Source provides no separate excerpt; meta description used. Replace if you prefer.
posts.featuredImageAlt: Security-awareness manager reviewing a campaign report and planning a follow-up training session.
posts.contentHtml:
The campaign is a beginning, not the finish line

A phishing simulation can produce useful information, but the value of the exercise depends on what the organisation does next. Reports can help identify message patterns, audience questions and topics that deserve more attention.

The next step should be practical, proportionate and connected to the learning objective.

Start with the pattern

Look across the campaign rather than focusing on one employee. Which message types led to more interaction? Were there departments that would benefit from clearer guidance? Did employees use the reporting route? Did technical factors affect the event data?

Review the available tracking signals carefully. Opens and clicks can be affected by email privacy features and automated security scanners, so do not interpret one metric in isolation.

Select a focused learning response

A useful follow-up does not need to be complicated. Examples include:

  • A short reminder about checking the sender and the request.
  • Guidance on hovering over or verifying unexpected links.
  • A team discussion about payment-change and sensitive-information requests.
  • A demonstration of how to report suspicious messages.
  • A training module that addresses the learning objective of the campaign.

Avoid overwhelming employees with too many topics at once. Choose the guidance that best matches the pattern you observed.

Make it easy to complete

Training should have a clear purpose and a reasonable expectation. Tell employees what they are meant to learn and where to go if they have questions. Where appropriate, record enrolment and completion so programme owners can understand whether the follow-up activity took place.

Measure progress over time

Repeat simulations thoughtfully and compare trends across similar exercises. Use consistent definitions and take changes in audience, template, timing and tracking setup into account. Look for broader improvement, including employee reporting behaviour and familiarity with the correct response process.

Use results respectfully

Employees should not be publicly ranked or embarrassed. Share individual details only with authorised people who need them, and use the findings to improve guidance and processes. A simulation is a learning tool, not a complete evaluation of a person's performance.

Phause brings campaign reporting, risk indicators and training administration together to help teams organise the follow-up process. Use campaign findings to choose a learning topic, manage the relevant module record and review completion history where available.
